title: Judge Says White House Cannot Ban News Outlets Over Their Coverage, for Now
summary:
A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that President Trump cannot ban news organizations from covering him at the White House just because he does not like their reporting. The ruling lasts at least until the case goes to a full trial.

Last month, the Trump administration took away the White House press passes of more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The three news organizations sued. In September, Judge Timothy J. Kelly gave them a temporary order letting their reporters back in while the case continued.

In his new decision, Kelly found that the ban likely broke the reporters' free speech rights in two ways. He also found it likely broke their right to due process, which means a fair warning and a fair chance to object before being punished. Both rights are part of the Bill of Rights in the U.S. Constitution.

The Justice Department had argued that the ban was about national security. Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, did not accept that argument. He pointed to the president's own public comments and social media posts. He wrote that Trump likely banned the reporters because he believes their reporting is inaccurate and unfair to him, and that this is a form of unlawful punishment.

Kelly also wrote that his decision does not mean Trump's concerns about fairness in the media are unfounded.

Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the news outlets, praised the ruling. He said the ban harmed his clients, free speech and the public. The White House did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.

The ruling did not settle one issue. CNN has sometimes been kept out of small spaces, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One, where only a few reporters can fit at once.
why_it_matters: The case tests whether a government can punish reporters for coverage it dislikes, which affects how freely the public can learn about its leaders.

background_read: The First Amendment, part of the Bill of Rights, protects freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.
Reporters who cover the president regularly carry White House press passes, which let them work in the press area and attend briefings.
When people believe the government has broken their rights, they can sue in federal court, where a judge can order a pause while the case goes on.
In this case, the president took away the passes of reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, and the news outlets went to court to get them back.
